answer: {{in.volts|int}} volts at {{in.amps|int}} amps is {{out.va|int}} VA, which is {{out.watts|int}} watts at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}} or {{out.va|int}} W for a heater. Watts = volts × amps × power factor. Volts alone do not give watts: you need the current too. On DC the power factor is one, so {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V at {{ex.0.in.amps|int}} A is {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} W.
how: {{out.volts|int}} V × {{in.amps|int}} A = {{out.va|int}} VA. × {{out.pf|2}} power factor = {{out.watts|int}} W of real power. On DC the power factor is one, so watts = volts × amps exactly; on three-phase the product is multiplied by √3 as well.
key_facts: Watts = volts × amps × power factor. {{in.volts|int}} V × {{in.amps|int}} A at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}} is {{out.watts|int}} W.
On DC there is no power factor: {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V × {{ex.0.in.amps|int}} A = {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} W and {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V × {{ex.1.in.amps|int}} A = {{ex.1.out.watts|int}} W.

At the same {{ex.2.in.amps|int}} A, a {{ex.2.in.volts|int}} V heater gives {{ex.2.out.watts|int}} W, while a {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V battery load gives a small fraction of that: higher voltage moves more power through the same current.
Voltage on its own is not power. A {{d.v_1ph|int}} V socket supplies only as many watts as the connected load draws in amps.

formula.text: P = V × I (DC);  P = V × I × PF (single-phase AC);  P = √3 × V × I × PF (three-phase AC);  Ohm's law: V = I × R
lines: PF = power factor (1 for DC and heaters)
R = resistance in ohms (Ω); V × I without PF is the apparent power in VA

p: Watts are volts times amps, adjusted by the power factor on AC. {{in.volts|int}} V × {{in.amps|int}} A = {{out.va|int}} VA; a heater turns all of it into {{out.va|int}} W, a motor at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}} only {{out.watts|int}} W of useful power.
Rearranged, the same formula gives amps = watts ÷ volts and volts = watts ÷ amps. The watts to amps calculator and the amps to watts calculator do those directions.

Volts alone have no watts. Voltage is the electrical pressure; watts appear only when current flows. A {{d.v_1ph|int}} V socket with nothing plugged in delivers zero watts; with {{in.amps|int}} A of heating load it delivers {{out.va|int}} W. The same applies to an older {{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V figure: {{ex.4.in.amps|int}} A there is {{ex.4.out.watts|int}} W at a power factor of one.

sections.h2: {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} volts to watts and other DC systems
p: For batteries, solar panels and car circuits choose DC. {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V × {{ex.0.in.amps|int}} A = {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} W, and {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V × {{ex.1.in.amps|int}} A = {{ex.1.out.watts|int}} W. A higher battery voltage carries the same power with fewer amps, which is why larger inverters run on higher-voltage banks.

sections.h2: Watts, volts, amps triangle and Ohm's law
p: The power triangle (P = V × I) links watts, volts and amps: cover the one you want and the other two show how to get it. Ohm's law (V = I × R) links volts, amps and resistance. Together they answer most circuit questions: for a pure resistance such as a heater element, watts also equal amps squared × ohms, and volts squared ÷ ohms.

Ohm's law applies directly only to resistive loads. Motors, chargers and LED drivers do not behave like a fixed resistance, so for them measure or read the current and use watts = volts × amps × power factor.

mistakes: Asking how many watts a voltage is. Voltage alone has no power; you need the current the load draws.
Multiplying volts × amps for a motor and calling it watts. That is VA; the real watts are lower by the power factor (about {{d.pf_mixed|2}}).
Using Ohm's law with a fixed resistance for a motor, charger or LED driver. Their resistance is not constant; use the measured current instead.
Forgetting √3 on three-phase. The {{d.v_3ph|int}} V row in the table already includes it.
safety: Measuring live voltage and current at the mains is dangerous. Use a clamp meter rated for the circuit, keep to battery and plug-in measurements yourself, and let a licensed electrician take readings inside a distribution board.

faq.q: How do I convert volts to watts?
faq.a: Multiply volts by amps, then by the power factor on AC. {{in.volts|int}} V × {{in.amps|int}} A × {{out.pf|2}} = {{out.watts|int}} W. Without the current there is no answer.
None on its own. Watts depend on the current: {{in.amps|int}} A at {{d.v_1ph|int}} V is {{out.va|int}} W for a heater and {{out.watts|int}} W for a motor at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}}.
It depends on the amps. At {{ex.0.in.amps|int}} A, {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V gives {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} W; double the current and the watts double.

faq.q: How do I convert volts to amps?
faq.a: Divide the watts by the volts (and the power factor on AC): amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor). The watts to amps calculator does this for DC, single-phase and three-phase.

faq.q: What is the watts, volts, amps triangle?
faq.a: Watts = volts × amps, volts = watts ÷ amps, amps = watts ÷ volts. On AC multiply the volts × amps side by the power factor.

faq.q: Is this an Ohm's law calculator?
faq.a: It covers the power side of Ohm's law: watts from volts and amps. Ohm's law itself, V = I × R, links volts, amps and resistance and holds exactly only for resistive loads such as heater elements.
